body:
- His wealth is about 90%+ D-Mart founder equity. His promoter stake is 67-82% depending on date, and the value of 14 listed holdings in June 2024 was about ₹2.14 lakh crore, which includes Avenue Supermarts. The replicable lesson from Damani is therefore mostly about business-building (cost discipline, owned real estate, fast working capital, slow expansion), not about stock-picking.
- The 1992 short was a very high-variance trade: he was squeezed by a manipulated bull market and survived on timing. Luck and staying power, not just analysis, explain that outcome.

body:
`person:mohnish-pabrai` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: us, india, process, cloning, concentration, cyclical

Pabrai Investment Funds since 1999. Long-run record is murky: an app-store bio claims >28% net since inception (unreliable); a profile says $100,000 at inception became $1.207m by 30 Jun 2017 (~14.8% annualised) - the more checkable figure. The funds reportedly fell ~60-70% peak-to-trough in 2008-09 (unverified). Process: 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much'; a few concentrated bets in simple businesses in distress; openly clone other great investors' positions (13Fs, Indian superstar filings); checklists built from past errors. Signature trades: Fiat Chrysler (~2012-18, large gain), Rain Industries (India; bought ~2015 at ~$0.60/share, i.e., about Rs 40, rose roughly 10x by early 2018 - it and Fiat were his most concentrated positions in Jan 2018 - then gave back most of the gain), US coal miners in 2021-22 (large gains, unverified). India book later: Edelweiss Financial (7-8% stake 2023-24, under 1% by Sep 2025), Sunteck Realty (~6.7%). Mistakes: Horsehead Holdings (zinc recycler, bankrupt 2016 - near total loss); round-trips in cyclical commodity names (Rain) when he did not sell near peak margins. Copyable: cloning as idea sourcing, a written checklist, few bets; but in cyclicals sell when margins and P/B are peak, not when P/E looks low.

body:
**Hidden trap: Satyam's 'cash-rich, debt-free' balance sheet** (`case_study:hidden-trap-satyam-cash`, verified). THE GOOD NUMBER: a debt-free IT exporter with ~Rs 5,000 cr+ of cash, growth, NYSE ADRs and a PwC audit; on screens it looked like one of India's safest balance sheets. WHY IT LIED: Raju confessed on 7 Jan 2009 that Rs 5,040 cr of the Rs 5,361 cr cash did not exist; Rs 376 cr of 'accrued interest' was invented; the SFIO found Satyam even paid tax on interest from non-existent fixed deposits (2000-01 to 2007-08) to keep the fiction consistent. TELLS THAT WERE PUBLIC: (1) cash that does not behave like cash: CLSA in Sep 2008 found it 'intriguing' that a company with ~$1.2 bn of cash closed FY08 with $56 m of debt; holding large cash while borrowing is irrational unless the cash is trapped or fake; (2) the cash never came back to shareholders (no large buyback/dividend); (3) promoter holding fell from ~25% to ~8.6% and was pledged; (4) the Dec-2008 attempt to spend $1.6 bn on promoter-family Maytas companies. TEST: compute interest income / average (cash + deposits) and compare with prevailing FD rates (~7-9% then); ask for bank confirmations by name; check that cash grows with retained CFO. LESSON: the strongest-looking number (cash) is the easiest to forge when the auditor relies on management-supplied confirmations.

**Hidden trap: Wirecard's fintech growth, margins and EUR 1.9 bn cash** (`case_study:hidden-trap-wirecard-margins-cash`, verified). THE GOOD NUMBER: a payments company growing 30%+ with high margins and a large cash pile, in the DAX, audited by EY for a decade. WHY IT LIED: about half of profits came through third-party acquirers (TPAs) in Asia that Wirecard did not own and that auditors could not see directly; EUR 1.9 bn of cash was said to sit in Philippine trustee accounts. On 18 Jun 2020 EY could not confirm it, on 22 Jun the company said it probably did not exist; insolvency 25 Jun 2020; shares -98%. TELLS: (1) margin and growth far above listed payment peers with lower take-rates in a competitive industry; (2) profits concentrated in an opaque, outsourced segment; (3) operating cash flow much weaker than EBITDA once customer-fund movements were removed; rising receivables; (4) expensive acquisitions in India/Asia paid to obscure funds; (5) the company and regulator (BaFin short-selling ban, complaints against FT journalists) attacked critics instead of producing evidence. TEST: insist that cash is held in the company's own name at a known bank; check whether the profitable segment is the same one you can verify; strip customer/merchant funds out of CFO. LESSON: high quality numbers that live in places you cannot audit are not high quality.
title: flags_judgment › Case notes

body:
1. **New-store investment vs capex gap** (§3.3). *Clears if* the tenant allowance is disclosed at ≥$0.4M per store, or a cohort payback table is published. *Confirms if* the next 10-K raises the $0.4M or quietly drops the payback sentence.
2. **Comp durability** (2-year stack ~+30% in H1 FY26). *Clears if* Q4 FY26 and FY27 comps stay positive against +15–23% comparisons, with transactions positive. *Confirms if* traffic turns negative while ticket carries the comp.
3. **Tariff regime and vendor pass-through.** The refund is one-off; replacement tariffs are possibly higher in 2027; the 60% domestic-vendor channel's refunds are unknown. *Clears if* merchandise margin holds in FY27 with tariffs at the new rates.
4. **Insider cluster selling** (Sep-2026, 5 insiders, $6M+). Low weight (L14). *Changes if* the CEO or CFO sell outside 10b5-1, or an insider buys at scale.
5. **Executive turnover** (CEO, 2 CFOs, CMO and other senior exits in 18 months). *Clears* after 4+ quarters with a stable team.
6. **Class action in discovery.** *Clears* on dismissal or settlement below ~1% of market cap.

**Count of open soft flags: 6** (plus a mechanical normalisation of FCF and GAAP EPS). That is above the 3+ rule, so *no position without a written variant view*. This is a statement about our evidence, not about the company.
**Hard disqualifiers found: none** (no restatement, no auditor change, no going-concern language, no related-party diversion).

body:
- Sona does not guide revenue ('we don't give forward growth guidance'). Its scoreable statements are mix targets (BEV share, non-auto share), a margin band and return ratios, so n is small (6 scored).
- The margin band drifted down in the open: 24-25% (Oct-25, met for FY26 at 24.7%) -> 23-25% (Apr-26) -> 'around 23%' (Oct-26). Each change was said out loud with a reason (railway consolidation, traction-motor mix, commodity lag). That is candour, not a goalpost move under the pilot rule.
- The one clear miss: 'recovery measures ... visible from quarter 2' (Jul-26) - Q2FY27 margin was flat at ~23% and management said so in the opening remarks.
- The non-auto >25% delivery is mostly mechanical (railway acquisition consolidated), so it says little about execution. Discount the +50 SAC accordingly - the shrink weight (0.23) already does most of that.
title: SONACOMS › 3. Reading

body:
Harsha's India engineering segment earns 22–24% EBITDA, but group ROIC ~11.5% and ROIIC ~11% (< 12.5% cost of equity) while
₹600 cr of capex goes in at ~54% subsidiary utilisation. **Rules:** compute group ROIC and ROIIC before reading segment margins;
rebuild capex payback two ways (current utilisation vs management's asset-turn claim). Report AGM dissent as
votes against ÷ (votes cast − promoter shares): a "14%" against was ~92% of non-promoter votes. L40 for manufacturers: the
government input is often subsidised financing or a dated rule (e.g. solar relaxations), possibly absent from the AR.
Process: take the frame close from the bhavcopy's date column, not the file name; card input validation (credibility as fraction).
**Pattern to watch:** 6 of 6 live cards = size 0 (EV below the 1.76x hurdle). Either the market is roughly fair on random draws
(expected) or the hurdle/tails make the card structurally say no. Check at the first scoring season before changing anything.
